title: How Immigration Works
summary: Josh and Chuck open with news that the DREAM Act passed the House (vote 216 to 198 is not stated; they say it passed) and heads to the Senate, which would offer a path to citizenship for certain children brought to the US illegally. They then give an overview of US immigration: Ellis Island history, the Department of Homeland Security and its agencies (USCIS, Customs and Border Protection), the difference between immigration and emigration, types of aliens, lawful permanent residence, family-sponsored and employment-based visas and preference categories, the diversity lottery, investor visas, asylum (affirmative and defensive, expedited removal), refugees (deferred to a future episode), illegal immigration and border issues, guest worker proposals, the Bracero program and Operation Wetback, and past amnesties. The episode closes with a listener mail shout-out for a friend's birthday.

segments.title: Opening banter and DREAM Act news
segments.summary: Hosts plug their podcast awards, social media, and then discuss the DREAM Act passing the House and moving to the Senate, which offers a path to citizenship for certain children brought to the US illegally, with conditions and a estimated federal deficit reduction.

segments.title: Ellis Island and immigrant ancestry
segments.summary: Hosts describe Ellis Island's history as a processing point for immigrants from 1892 to 1954, with about twelve million passing through, and note that many Americans descend from those immigrants.

segments.title: Nativism and attending a naturalization ceremony
segments.summary: Chuck distinguishes nativists from Native Americans and recounts attending a naturalization ceremony in Los Angeles connected to a documentary about actress Jane Seymour's naturalization.

segments.title: Immigration agencies and terminology
segments.summary: The hosts explain immigration versus emigration, the shift from the INS to Department of Homeland Security after 2001, and the roles of Customs and Border Protection and USCIS. Congress sets immigration law while the president directs refugee policy. Alien terminology is covered: illegal alien, legal alien, resident alien, nonresident alien, naturalized citizen.

segments.title: Lawful permanent residence and the visa process
segments.summary: The hosts explain lawful permanent residency as allowing one to live and work in the US permanently without citizenship rights, and describe the visa application process, consular interviews, and port-of-entry screening, with differences between temporary and permanent visas.

segments.title: Family-based immigration and preference categories
segments.summary: The hosts describe family sponsorship: immediate relatives of citizens need no visa number, while other family categories (spouses and unmarried children of permanent residents, married children of citizens, siblings of adult citizens) have numerical preferences. An affidavit of support is required at 125 percent of the poverty line.

segments.title: Diversity lottery, employment visas, and investor visas
segments.summary: The diversity visa lottery is described as a program for people from countries with low US immigration, with about 55,000 visas. Employment-based immigration involves labor certification and petitions, with EB-1 through EB-4 categories. Investor visas offer 10,000 visas a year for investments creating ten or more jobs, with a portion set aside for regional centers in rural areas.

segments.title: Asylum: affirmative, defensive, and expedited removal
segments.summary: Asylum is explained as protection for people fleeing persecution based on race, religion, nationality, political opinion, or social group, rooted in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the 1980 Refugee Act. Affirmative asylum is applied for at a port within a year and is non-adversarial; defensive asylum occurs in court during deportation proceedings. Expedited removal applies to people caught without documents, who are asked four screening questions.

segments.title: Refugees (deferred)
segments.summary: The hosts note refugee policy is set by the president and cite about 13.6 million refugees worldwide in 2009 and US admissions of about 60,000 refugees last year, and agree to do a separate refugee episode later.

segments.title: Illegal immigration, border dangers, and guest workers
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the estimated 10.8 million illegal immigrants, dangers in border crossings and smuggling by coyotes, Mexico drug war violence, the argument over immigrant taxes and remittances, the proposed guest worker program, and the historical Bracero program and Operation Wetback in 1954, when over a million Mexican nationals were deported.

segments.title: Amnesty history and border fence
segments.summary: The hosts list past amnesties, including the 1980 Mariel boatlift Cubans, Nicaraguans under the Central American Relief Act, Haitian refugees, and the 1986 Immigration Reform and Control Act under Reagan covering about 2.8 million. They also mention the border fence of about 580 miles and the Minutemen Civil Defense Corps.

segments.title: Listener mail: birthday shout-out for Alona
segments.summary: A listener named Eric asks for a shout-out for a friend Alona's birthday, after collecting messages from artists such as Andrew Bird and Priscilla Ono. The hosts read the request and promise a mention.
